summary:
Space Mission Designer is a free browser game where anyone, even primary-school kids, can plan a NASA-style space mission and learn why each engineering choice matters. Players pick a target (Moon, Venus, Mars, Psyche, Europa or Titan), science goals and an orbit, then build a spacecraft: rocket, power source, battery, flight computer, attitude control, radiation shield, antenna, ground station and instruments. Every part has a cost, so players balance budget, mass, power, radiation, communications, data and mission lifetime across 12 engineering checks. After launch, the spacecraft faces space events like solar storms. A report card explains every result in plain words and shows the real NASA mission closest to the player's design. Successful missions unlock Science Run, a mini game where players fly their own spacecraft.

In class, students usually only see the launch. Our game lets them make the trade-offs themselves, so a fact like "sunlight at Saturn is 90× weaker" becomes something they experience, not just memorize. It runs on any computer or phone with no install, and is built on real NASA data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Space Mission Designer is a free browser game that walks players through the same decisions a NASA mission team makes. A game has four steps:

1. Plan: pick a target (the Moon, Venus, Mars, the asteroid Psyche, Europa or Titan), science goals and an orbit.

2. Build: choose a rocket, power source, battery, flight computer, attitude control, radiation shield, antenna, ground station and science instruments. The spacecraft drawing changes with every part, and colored bars show budget, mass, power and data at a glance. When something is wrong, a "Fix it" button jumps straight to the part that needs attention.

3. Launch: a countdown and flight animation, with random space events (solar storms, cosmic ray bursts, micrometeoroid strikes) that the design must survive.

4. Learn: a report card scores 12 engineering checks (budget, schedule, payload, power, battery, radiation, communications, data downlink, pointing, coverage, mission lifetime and science), explains every result in plain words, and shows which of 13 real NASA missions (from Lunar Prospector to Dragonfly) is closest to the player's design.

Successful missions unlock Science Run, a mini game where players fly their own spacecraft, collect science data and send it home to Earth.

BENEFITS

- Students make real engineering trade-offs instead of memorizing facts. A bigger instrument needs more power, more power means more mass, and more mass needs a stronger rocket.

- Free, with no install and no account: it runs in any browser on a computer, tablet or phone, so a teacher can share one link with the whole class.

- Four difficulty levels (Easy, Normal, Hard, Sandbox) fit young beginners and older students.

- Space School has a glossary and a short lesson for every check, and "Why? (Learn more)" boxes give curious players the technical details.

- Share links let a student send their spacecraft to a friend, who can open it, improve it and fly it.

INTENDED IMPACT

In class, students usually only see the launch. We want them to understand that a space mission is a chain of connected choices, and that engineering means balancing limits like money, time, mass and power. Every report card points to a real NASA mission, so players have a next step to read about. Our goal is to make kids curious about space science and engineering careers, starting at primary-school age.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Game logic: Python (pure functions with a built-in self-test, so every rule is in one place)

- Backend: FastAPI and Uvicorn (JSON API and leaderboards)

- Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion

- Art and sound: rocket and spacecraft drawings generated as SVG in Python; all sound effects and music generated in code with the Web Audio API (no audio files)

- Deployment: Docker on Render; code on GitHub

- Pitch deck: Reveal.js, hosted on Netlify

- Development: VS Code, Git, and Claude Code (an AI coding assistant) for writing and reviewing code. Our team made the game design decisions, checked the values against NASA sources and play-tested the game.

- Hardware: only our own laptops; players need nothing but a browser.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- The spacecraft you design is the ship you fly. In Science Run, the flight computer sets your memory, the antenna sets how fast data goes home, the shield gives you armor and the total mass decides how agile you are.

- Real physics, made simple: solar panels get weaker far from the Sun but an RTG does not, so a player who goes to Titan with solar panels discovers why NASA chose nuclear power for missions to the outer planets.

- Hard mode adds a random surprise, such as a budget cut, a launch window delay, a solar maximum or a bigger science goal, just like real missions face.

- Players see their own design next to a real NASA mission, so they learn how close they came to what NASA actually built.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Age and reading level: short sentences, colored bars and 1-3 emoji ratings instead of raw numbers; the details are optional.

- Real but simple science: values are based on public NASA data, and rules are simplified without being wrong.

- Balance: every mission can be completed on every difficulty and with every Hard-mode surprise, but never by accident.

- Access: free hosting, a mobile layout with touch controls, and options for sound, music and animation.

- Fairness and privacy: players enter only a nickname. A borrowed design has to be changed before it can enter the leaderboard.

- Maintainability: all game math lives in one Python module, so the rules are easy to test and adjust.
